title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing -- August 20, 2026 (Floor-Limitation and Placeholder-Correction Cycle)
headline: Five countries scored zero of 100 tonight, and the scale has no lower number left to give them.
summary: Five countries were checked again tonight and stayed exactly where they were: zero of 100, the lowest score the benchmark can give. Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen, Israel and Myanmar each have all eight of the benchmark's measured areas, and all forty more detailed checks inside them, sitting at the lowest possible reading. New harm kept arriving -- a Sudanese army strike that killed at least 35 people at a court in North Darfur, 36 aid workers killed in South Sudan since January, Myanmar's own air force killing 14 civilians in one village -- but none of it could move a score that has no room left to fall. Two more countries, Somalia and Haiti, have only about five points of room left, below the threshold the benchmark needs to file a formal finding. The Democratic Republic of the Congo has even less. Two findings tonight rest on real, individual conduct: Kazakhstan, where a journalist was sentenced to eight years in prison ahead of an election, crossed into the benchmark's lowest performance band -- the only one of five proposed band crossings tonight to pass the benchmark's evidence test. Zambia fell for a third straight review after its own human-rights commission was denied access to a detainee. Five companies were measured individually for the first time tonight, after each had shared one never-checked starting score with ten or more competitors. Two of the five, IDEXX Laboratories and ManpowerGroup, turned up no evidence of wrongdoing in either direction; their lower numbers measure what had never been checked, not new misconduct. A sixth finding, Interpublic Group, is not really about a score at all: the company was bought by Omnicom in a merger completed in November 2025 and no longer exists as an independent company. Nothing was applied to the published rankings tonight.

pipeline.queueHandling: Twenty organizations were checked tonight. Seven findings were filed and thirteen scores were confirmed unchanged. None of the seven were applied to the published rankings. Five countries already sit at the lowest possible score, with every measured area at the floor, so no further downgrade could be filed for them even where new harm was documented. Two findings rest on the entity's own conduct: Kazakhstan, after a journalist was sentenced to eight years in prison, and Zambia, after Zambia's own human rights commission was denied access to a detainee. Five findings are first-time measurements of companies that had shared one never-checked starting score with ten or more peers; two of those five turned up no evidence of wrongdoing in either direction, and a third, Interpublic Group, no longer exists as an independent company after a completed merger.

topSignals.title: Five Countries Scored Zero of 100 Tonight, With No Lower Number Left to Give Them
topSignals.whyItMatters: Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen, Israel and Myanmar already sit at the benchmark's lowest possible score. New harm keeps arriving, but the scale has no room left to record it -- a limit of the measurement tool, not a sign nothing happened.
topSignals.description: Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen, Israel and Myanmar were all checked again tonight and confirmed at zero of 100, the lowest score the benchmark can assign. Every one of the eight areas the benchmark measures, and all forty more detailed checks inside them, already sits at the lowest possible reading for each country. That is why real, documented harm this cycle could not move any of the five scores. A Sudanese army drone strike killed at least 35 people at a traditional court in North Darfur on 2 August -- this review corrected the initial account, which had blamed a paramilitary group rather than Sudan's own armed forces. In South Sudan, 36 aid workers and contractors have been killed since January, already more than died in all of 2025. In Israel, the United Nations told the Security Council the West Bank is "at the breaking point," citing more than 1,430 settler incidents in 2026. In Myanmar, the country's own air force killed 14 civilians, aged 9 to 88, in raids on one village. None of it moved a score that was already at zero. Two more countries, Somalia (5.0) and Haiti (3.1), have only about five points of room left to fall -- below the threshold the benchmark needs to file a formal finding even when new harm is confirmed. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (2.5) has less than half that room. This is the second consecutive review confirming Sudan at the floor, and the pattern now spans eight of the twenty countries and companies checked tonight.

evidence.quote: At least 35 people were killed and dozens more injured in a drone strike by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) on a traditional court on Sunday afternoon.
evidence.claim: A 2 August strike on a North Darfur court, initially attributed to a paramilitary group, was carried out by Sudan's own armed forces.

evidence.quote: The West Bank is at the breaking point
evidence.claim: The UN told the Security Council that settler violence in the West Bank had reached what officials called an all-time high, citing more than 1,430 incidents in 2026.
evidence.source: UN Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process (UNSCO)

topSignals.title: Kazakhstan Crosses Into the Benchmark's Lowest Band After a Journalist Is Sentenced to Eight Years
topSignals.whyItMatters: Kazakhstan's score had never been individually checked before tonight. The real number is lower than the placeholder it replaces, and it is the only band crossing tonight to pass the benchmark's evidence test.
topSignals.description: Kazakhstan's published score of 20.3 was never based on an individual review. It was a placeholder number shared, digit for digit, with eleven other countries, from Algeria to Zimbabwe. Tonight's review is the first real measurement, and it lands at 13.7 of 100 -- low enough to cross from the Developing band into the Critical band. An Almaty court sentenced Gulnara Bazhkenova, the former editor-in-chief of the independent outlet Orda, to eight years in prison on 18 August, plus a five-year ban on journalism, blogging and public engagement. Since late July, Kazakhstan has also arrested a political satirist, sentenced three more journalists, and coordinated the removal of a dozen leading journalists' accounts, according to a joint statement from nine press-freedom and rights organizations. The UN Human Rights Committee, reviewing Kazakhstan in July, recorded concern about the use of force and torture against civil-society members. Kazakhstan does run a real social safety net -- about 163,000 people receive targeted assistance -- which is why it still scores above regional peers Azerbaijan (9.4) and Tajikistan (7.8). This is the only one of five band-crossing findings filed tonight to pass the benchmark's evidence test, which requires an independent, entity-specific finding at a high enough source tier. Kazakhstan's 23 August parliamentary election is a scheduled future event and was not scored as conduct. The finding is filed and recorded, not applied. Kazakhstan's published score is unchanged.

evidence.quote: Kazakhstan sentences journalist Gulnara Bazhkenova to eight years in prison as pre-election press crackdown intensifies
evidence.claim: An Almaty court sentenced the former editor-in-chief of the independent outlet Orda to eight years in prison on 18 August 2026, with a five-year ban on media, journalism, blogging and public engagement.

evidence.quote: use of force and acts of torture against members of civil society
evidence.claim: The UN Human Rights Committee, reviewing Kazakhstan in July 2026, recorded concern about the use of force and torture against civil-society members and urged Kazakhstan to narrow the criminal-code provision suppressing protected speech.
evidence.source: UN Human Rights Committee Concluding Observations (July 2026), reproduced by Amnesty International

topSignals.title: Zambia Falls for a Third Straight Review After Its Own Rights Commission Is Denied Access to a Detainee
topSignals.whyItMatters: This is not a one-off dip. Zambia has scored below its published number in three consecutive reviews, each time on the government's own conduct rather than an outside event.
topSignals.description: Zambia's review lands at 28.7 of 100, down from a published 35.9, while staying inside the Developing band. This is the third review in a row to land below the published score: 33.1 on 31 July, 31.9 on 18 August, and 28.7 tonight. The UN's top human rights official, Volker Turk, publicly urged Zambia on 19 August to stop arbitrary arrests and tell detainees why they were held, warning that the country's democratic credentials are at risk. Days earlier, police denied Zambia's own Human Rights Commission access to a detainee, businessman Valden Harry Findlay, who was held with sixteen others after President Hakainde Hichilema's re-election on 13 August. Blocking the country's own oversight body from doing its job is scored as Zambia's own conduct, not as an outside event. The finding is filed and recorded, not applied. Zambia's published score is unchanged.

evidence.quote: due process and ensure detainees are informed of the reasons for their arrest
evidence.claim: The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights publicly called on Zambia to stop arbitrary arrests and tell detainees why they were held.
evidence.source: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

topSignals.title: Five Companies Are Measured Individually for the First Time -- Two Show No Evidence of Wrongdoing at All
topSignals.whyItMatters: A large drop from a placeholder score is not the same as a finding that a company got worse. Two of tonight's five first-time measurements turned up zero adverse evidence in either direction.
topSignals.description: Hyatt Hotels, IDEXX Laboratories, InterContinental Hotel and ManpowerGroup were all measured individually for the first time tonight, after each had shared a never-checked starting score with ten or more competitors -- 77.9 for Hyatt and IDEXX, and 60.9 for InterContinental and ManpowerGroup, a number shared across 22 companies, three of which were already corrected on 18 August. IDEXX Laboratories and ManpowerGroup are the cleanest cases: no regulatory finding, lawsuit, labor dispute or complaint of any kind was located for either company, in either direction. Their lower readings -- 45.6 and 46.9 -- measure what the benchmark had never checked, mainly because both companies publish little of the workforce data the benchmark looks for, not because either company did something wrong. InterContinental Hotel is different: it carries a real, documented pattern of not answering independent labor allegations, including reports of migrant-worker exploitation and of hotels replacing striking workers with vulnerable migrants, which is why its reading (34.4) crossed two performance bands down to Developing rather than one. Hyatt Hotels landed at 44.4 on a thinner, largely self-published evidence base. All four crossed a published band line tonight, and all four failed the benchmark's evidence test for a band crossing, because the strongest evidence behind each is still the shared placeholder score, not an outside finding naming the company by name. Four of tonight's five company findings, including all four described here, are marked low or medium confidence and are recorded as needing a further, targeted evidence pass before any decision is made. None of the five findings have been applied. Published scores are unchanged.

evidence.claim: IDEXX Laboratories published its 2025 Corporate Responsibility Report in July 2026; no adverse finding about the company, in either direction, was located.

IHG hotels have been reported, without a public response from the company, to have replaced striking workers with vulnerable migrants, including children, who were then subject to long hours, few breaks and wage theft.

topSignals.title: Interpublic Group's Finding Is Held Back by a Bigger Problem: the Company No Longer Exists
topSignals.whyItMatters: Omnicom completed its purchase of Interpublic Group in November 2025. Publishing a standalone score for a company that no longer independently exists would be misleading, whatever the number.
topSignals.description: Interpublic Group's review lands at 31.3 of 100, down from a published 40.0, staying inside the Developing band. But the number is not the point. Omnicom Group's acquisition of Interpublic Group, agreed in December 2024, was completed in November 2025. Interpublic Group no longer exists as an independent company, so its standalone entry in the Fortune 500 index is a stale record that needs a decision before any score is applied -- the same kind of defect already fixed once this cycle when a duplicate "Automatic Data Process" entry was merged into ADP on 17 August. The underlying evidence still splits cleanly by company: 3,200 jobs Interpublic Group cut in 2025 while it was still independent are scored as its own conduct; more than 4,000 further job cuts and several retired advertising brands, announced by Omnicom after the deal closed, are Omnicom's conduct and are not scored against Interpublic Group. The finding is filed and recorded. It should not be applied until the entity record is resolved.

evidence.claim: Omnicom Group's acquisition of Interpublic Group, agreed in December 2024, was completed in November 2025; Interpublic Group no longer exists as an independent company.

topSignals.title: Venezuela's Score Was Checked Against an Argument for an Upgrade -- and the Argument Was Rejected
topSignals.whyItMatters: A tempting argument said Venezuela's score should rise because it predates the departure of former president Nicolas Maduro. Checking the dates showed that argument was wrong, and the confirmation held.
topSignals.description: Venezuela's interim government announced the release of 131 political prisoners on 14-15 August, under a program named for peace and democratic coexistence. A closer check found a reason to doubt an upgrade rather than support one: independent verifiers Foro Penal and Vente Venezuela could confirm only 40 to 43 of those releases, against 391 people Foro Penal says remain detained. Scoring the independently verified floor, not the government's own claim, is why Venezuela's reading moved by just 0.1 point, to 18.1 from a published 18.0. A separate argument was raised and rejected this cycle: that Venezuela's score should be treated as outdated because it predates the removal of former president Nicolas Maduro. Maduro was removed on 3 January 2026; the published 18.0 was set on 19 April 2026 and confirmed twice more in July, all after the transition and all reflecting the current government's own conduct. The same discipline caught two other problems before they could reach print tonight: two candidates initially drafted for review were dropped after a source-date check found their headline events were dated one and two years earlier than first assumed.

evidence.claim: Venezuela's interim government announced 131 political-prisoner releases; independent monitors verified a much smaller number against hundreds still detained.

sectorAlerts.sector: Countries -- A Floor Finding Spans Five Nations, and Two More Have Almost No Room Left
sectorAlerts.headline: Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen, Israel and Myanmar all confirmed at zero of 100; Somalia and Haiti have less than five points of room to fall.
observations: Sudan (0.0): a state-military drone strike killed at least 35 people at a North Darfur court; the initial account had wrongly blamed a paramilitary group.
South Sudan (0.0), Yemen (0.0), Israel (0.0) and Myanmar (0.0): each confirmed at the arithmetic floor, with all forty of the benchmark's detailed measures already at the lowest anchor.
Somalia (5.0) and Haiti (3.1): both sit within about five points of the floor, below the threshold needed to file a formal downgrade even when new harm is documented.
Democratic Republic of the Congo (2.5): confirmed near the floor; its published index entry is truncated to "Democratic Republic of C," a naming defect logged for correction, with no score effect.

Kazakhstan (20.3 published, 13.7 proposed) and Zambia (35.9 published, 28.7 proposed): the only two countries this cycle where new, dated evidence of the government's own conduct produced a genuine finding.

methodologyNotes.name: A Score at the Bottom of the Scale Cannot Register Further Decline
methodologyNotes.description: Five countries confirmed tonight -- Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen, Israel and Myanmar -- already have every one of the benchmark's eight measured areas, and all forty more detailed checks inside them, at the lowest possible reading. When new harm is documented for a country already at that floor, it is recorded in the assessment record but cannot move the published score, because there is no lower number left to give. Two more countries, Somalia and Haiti, have less than the five points of room the benchmark needs to file a formal finding at all. This is a limitation of the measurement scale, not a finding that nothing happened.

methodologyNotes.name: A Score That Has Never Been Individually Measured Is Not the Same as a Score That Has Gotten Worse
methodologyNotes.description: Dozens of entities across the benchmark's indexes were assigned one identical starting score when their index was first built, before any individual review took place. Hyatt Hotels, IDEXX Laboratories, InterContinental Hotel and ManpowerGroup all fit this pattern tonight. Two of the four -- IDEXX Laboratories and ManpowerGroup -- show no adverse evidence of any kind; their lower readings measure what a placeholder score had never checked, not new misconduct.

methodologyNotes.name: A Band-Crossing Finding Must Pass an Evidence Test Before It Is Filed, and the Result Is Published Either Way
methodologyNotes.description: When a proposed score crosses a published band line, the benchmark checks whether at least one independent, non-self-published source makes a finding specific to that entity, at a high enough source tier. Kazakhstan's finding passed tonight, on a United Nations treaty-body finding and an eight-year prison sentence naming the country directly. Four other proposed crossings -- Hyatt Hotels, IDEXX Laboratories, InterContinental Hotel and ManpowerGroup -- did not pass, because the strongest evidence behind each is still a shared, never-measured placeholder score. All four are published as failed tests, not suppressed or softened.

methodologyNotes.name: A Company That No Longer Exists Independently Needs an Entity-Record Decision Before a Score Applies
methodologyNotes.description: Interpublic Group was acquired by Omnicom Group in a merger completed in November 2025 and no longer exists as an independent company. Its standalone entry in the Fortune 500 index is a stale record. The same defect was corrected once already this cycle window, when a duplicate Automatic Data Process entry was merged into ADP on 17 August. Interpublic Group's finding is filed and recorded, but should not be applied until the entity record itself is resolved.

dailyOpeningQuestion.text: IDEXX Laboratories fell 32.3 points tonight on zero adverse evidence, while Sudan's confirmed state-military strike on a North Darfur court produced no score movement at all. Does the benchmark's absence-of-disclosure convention move scores more readily than documented, severe state conduct at the floor?
dailyOpeningQuestion.tensionFraming: Same benchmark, opposite ends of the evidence-sensitivity problem.
